questions.title: Agile vs. Waterfall, blended
questions.prompt: A teammate tells you the company runs 'two-week sprints with a daily standup, but the original project charter and budget were signed off months ago in one big upfront document.' Is this company Agile, Waterfall, or something else, and why does that combination actually make sense?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a hybrid approach, and it's extremely common in real companies, not a contradiction. Waterfall plans an entire project up front in fixed phases — the charter and budget sign-off described here is a classic Waterfall step, useful for executive buy-in and setting an overall budget before work starts. Agile breaks the actual build into short, repeating cycles (sprints) where a team plans a slice of work, builds it, reviews it, and adapts — which is what the two-week sprints and daily standup describe. Combining them lets a company keep Waterfall's predictability for funding and sign-off while still getting Agile's ability to adjust as requirements become clearer during the actual build. Few companies are purely one model; this blend is the norm, not the exception.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them this is a hybrid shop, and that's actually a sign of a reasonably mature process, not confusion. The charter and budget sign-off up front is pure Waterfall — it exists because executives need a number and a scope before they'll fund something. But locking the entire technical design before any work starts is risky for most product-style work, so the actual build runs in Agile sprints instead, which lets the team adjust as they learn more. I'd also point out that hearing both vocabularies at once — 'the charter is approved, let's get it into the backlog for sprint planning' — is exactly what you'd expect to hear at a company like this, and it's not a red flag.
questions.example: A typical hybrid: a six-week Waterfall-style charter and budgeting phase up front, followed by five two-week Agile sprints for the actual build, closed out with a Waterfall-style UAT sign-off before launch. The scope and budget are fixed early; the technical details of how it's built flex sprint to sprint.
commonMistakes: Assuming a company has to be purely Agile or purely Waterfall
Thinking sprints and standups alone make an entire company 'Agile'
Not recognizing that most real companies land somewhere in between
Treating 'charter' and 'sprint' as contradictory vocabulary instead of two halves of a normal hybrid process
keyPoints: Waterfall = sequential, fixed phases, planned up front
Agile = iterative, short repeating cycles that adapt as work proceeds
A hybrid keeps Waterfall's upfront charter/budget and Agile's iterative build
Hearing both vocabularies at one company is normal in a hybrid shop

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as a hybrid approach
Explains why the hybrid makes sense for budgeting and iteration
Notes the mixed vocabulary as supporting evidence

questions.title: OSI model vs. TCP/IP model
questions.prompt: Why do networking engineers still reference the 7-layer OSI model when the TCP/IP model the real internet runs on only has 4 layers? What is each model actually good for?
questions.modelAnswer: The OSI model is a conceptual, teaching reference — it breaks networking into 7 granular layers and gives the field a shared vocabulary, which is exactly why phrases like 'that's a Layer 3 problem' or 'a Layer 7 load balancer' are OSI terms still used constantly in practice. The TCP/IP model is the practical model the actual internet protocol suite implements, with only 4 layers: link, internet, transport, and application. TCP/IP's application layer collapses OSI's session, presentation, and application layers into one, and TCP/IP's link layer collapses OSI's physical and data link layers into one. Neither model is 'more correct' — OSI gives precise troubleshooting vocabulary, TCP/IP describes what's actually implemented.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of OSI as the vocabulary and TCP/IP as the implementation. When I say a problem is 'Layer 4' or someone mentions a 'Layer 7 firewall,' they're using OSI's more granular layer numbers, even on a network that's actually running the 4-layer TCP/IP stack end to end. The mapping that actually matters: OSI's top three layers (session, presentation, application) all fold into TCP/IP's single application layer, and OSI's bottom two (physical, data link) fold into TCP/IP's single link layer. I'd never say one model is correct and the other isn't — they solve different problems, one for teaching and troubleshooting precision, one for describing what's genuinely implemented.
questions.example:
OSI: Application / Presentation / Session / Transport / Network / Data Link / Physical
TCP/IP: Application (= OSI's top three) / Transport / Internet (= OSI's Network) / Link (= OSI's bottom two)
commonMistakes: Thinking OSI is literally implemented in hardware or software somewhere
Conflating the layer numbers between the two models directly
Not knowing which OSI layers collapse into which TCP/IP layers
Forgetting both are reference models, not rigid constraints on how real systems must be built
keyPoints: OSI = 7-layer conceptual/teaching reference model
TCP/IP = 4-layer practical model the real internet implements
OSI's top three layers collapse into TCP/IP's application layer
OSI's bottom two layers collapse into TCP/IP's link layer
'Layer 4'/'Layer 7' vocabulary comes from OSI even on TCP/IP networks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains OSI's role as a teaching/reference model
Explains TCP/IP's role as the practical implemented model
Correctly maps which OSI layers collapse into which TCP/IP layers

questions.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and the shared responsibility model
questions.prompt: What's the difference between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, and how does the shared responsibility model's split between provider and customer change as you move from one to the other?
questions.modelAnswer: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) rents raw infrastructure — a VM like an Azure VM or EC2 instance — where the customer manages everything from the OS up: patching, runtime, application, and data. PaaS (Platform as a Service) — Azure App Service, a managed database — has the provider manage the OS and runtime, leaving the customer responsible for application code, configuration, and data. SaaS (Software as a Service) — Microsoft 365, Salesforce — is a fully managed application, where the provider manages nearly everything except the customer's own data and who has access to it. As you move IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, the customer's operational burden shrinks, but one thing never moves: the customer is always responsible for identity, access, and data classification, no matter which service model they're using.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as a sliding scale of 'what do I still have to manage myself.' With an IaaS VM, I'm patching the OS, managing the runtime, everything — the provider just gives me the hardware and hypervisor. With PaaS, say an Azure App Service, the platform handles the OS and runtime patching for me, and I'm only responsible for my application code and its configuration. With SaaS, like Office 365, I'm not managing any infrastructure or application code at all — I'm just responsible for my data and who on my team has access to it. The one constant across all three, and the thing people most often forget, is that identity and access management is never outsourced — that's always on the customer, regardless of which service model they're using.
questions.example:
IaaS: Azure VM, AWS EC2 — customer manages OS up.
PaaS: Azure App Service, AWS RDS — provider manages OS/runtime, customer manages app + data.
SaaS: Microsoft 365, Salesforce — provider manages nearly everything except data and access.
commonMistakes: Assuming the provider handles everything regardless of service model
Thinking identity and access management is ever fully outsourced to the provider
Confusing a managed VM (still IaaS) with a genuine PaaS offering
Treating the three models as three fixed buckets instead of a gradient of shrinking customer responsibility
keyPoints: IaaS = rent infrastructure, manage OS and everything above it
PaaS = provider manages OS/runtime, customer manages app code and data
SaaS = fully managed application, customer manages data and user access
Customer always owns identity, access, and data classification regardless of model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS with real examples
Correctly explains how responsibility shifts across the three models
Notes the customer always owns identity and data

lessonLink.label: Review: IaaS, PaaS & SaaS

questions.title: The Azure RBAC role-assignment equation
questions.prompt: Azure RBAC access control comes down to one equation combining three things. What are they, and why does changing just the scope change the entire effective role assignment, even if the security principal and role definition stay exactly the same?
questions.modelAnswer: Every Azure permission comes down to Role assignment = Security principal + Role definition + Scope. The security principal is the 'who' (a user, group, service principal, or managed identity), the role definition is the 'what' (a collection of permitted actions), and scope is the 'where' (management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource) the permission actually applies to. Scope matters enormously because it decides the real-world reach of the exact same role: assigning Contributor to the same person at the subscription level grants them control over every resource group in that subscription, while assigning that identical role at one resource group scope limits them to only that resource group. Same principal, same role definition, completely different real access, because scope changed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always come back to that equation when access questions come up: who, what, and where. The 'who' and 'what' get most of the attention in conversation, but scope is where the real risk usually hides. If I assign Alex the Contributor role at the subscription scope instead of at one resource group, Alex now has full management access to every resource group in that subscription, not just their project — same role name, dramatically different real access. Scope also inherits downward: a role assigned at a management group or subscription flows automatically into every resource group and resource underneath it, which is exactly why I always scope as narrow as the job actually requires.
questions.example: Alex needs to manage VMs in the finance app's resource group only. Assigning Contributor at the subscription scope would also give Alex access to every other resource group in that subscription. Assigning Contributor at just rg-finance-app's scope gives Alex exactly the access needed, and nothing more.
commonMistakes: Thinking the role name alone determines someone's access, ignoring scope
Forgetting scope is part of the equation at all
Assuming Owner and Contributor differ only in 'more permissions' rather than Owner's unique ability to grant access to others
Not realizing a role assigned at a higher scope is automatically inherited by everything underneath it
keyPoints: Role assignment = security principal + role definition + scope
Scope has four levels — management group, subscription, resource group, resource — inheriting downward
Owner can grant access to others; Contributor cannot
The same principal and role at a different scope is a functionally different assignment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the role-assignment equation
Explains scope's effect and downward inheritance
Correctly distinguishes Owner from Contributor

questions.title: IAM users vs. IAM roles
questions.prompt: What's the fundamental difference between an IAM user and an IAM role in AWS, and why does AWS guidance consistently recommend roles over long-lived user access keys for anything running on AWS infrastructure?
questions.modelAnswer: An IAM user is a permanent identity that can have a password and long-lived access keys, which keep working until someone manually deactivates or deletes them. An IAM role has no password and no permanent access keys of its own — instead it's assumed temporarily by a trusted entity (a user, an application, or an AWS service like EC2), governed by a trust policy that defines exactly who or what is allowed to assume it. When a role is assumed, AWS's Security Token Service (STS) issues short-lived temporary credentials that expire automatically, with no manual cleanup or rotation schedule needed. Roles beat long-lived keys because they eliminate an entire category of risk: there's no static secret sitting in a config file that can leak from a laptop or a public repo and keep working indefinitely for whoever has it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd put it: a user is an identity somebody owns permanently, a role is an identity nobody owns — it just gets borrowed temporarily. The classic example that makes this click is an EC2 instance reading from S3. The tempting shortcut is generating an IAM user access key and pasting it into the app's config — now there's a long-lived secret sitting on disk that can leak. The better pattern is a role with an S3-read policy, a trust policy letting EC2 assume it, attached to the instance as an instance profile. STS hands out temporary credentials behind the scenes automatically, and if that instance gets terminated, there's nothing left to revoke, because there was never a static key to leak in the first place.
questions.example: An EC2 instance needs to read from S3. Instead of generating an IAM user access key and hardcoding it, create a role with an s3:GetObject policy, give it a trust policy allowing the EC2 service to assume it, and attach it to the instance as an instance profile. No access key is ever generated, stored, or capable of leaking.
commonMistakes: Thinking a role is just 'a user with no password' rather than a fundamentally different, temporary identity
Forgetting a role needs a trust policy defining who or what can actually assume it
Assuming long-lived access keys aren't a significant real risk
Not knowing AWS STS is specifically what issues the temporary credentials
keyPoints: IAM user = permanent identity, optionally with long-lived access keys
IAM role = temporary identity, assumed, gated by a trust policy
AWS STS issues short-lived credentials when a role is assumed
Roles eliminate the entire risk category of a leaked static secret

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes IAM users from IAM roles
Correctly explains the STS/trust-policy mechanism
Explains why roles reduce real-world risk

lessonLink.label: Review: IAM Roles and Why They Beat Long-Lived Keys

questions.title: Security Groups vs. Network ACLs
questions.prompt: In AWS, why does a Network ACL need an explicit outbound rule for the ephemeral port range to let return traffic through, while a Security Group never needs a rule like that at all?
questions.modelAnswer: A Security Group is stateful: if it allows inbound traffic on a port, the matching response traffic back out is automatically allowed too, with no separate outbound rule required at all. A Network ACL is stateless: each direction is evaluated completely independently, so allowing inbound traffic on a port does nothing for the return traffic in the other direction. That's exactly why a NACL needs an explicit outbound allow rule covering the high ephemeral port range (1024-65535) — the client's response traffic comes back on one of those high ports, and without that rule it has nowhere to go and gets dropped, even though the original inbound request was allowed in just fine.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the detail that trips people up coming from Security Groups. With an SG, I write one inbound rule for port 443 and I'm done — the SG remembers that connection and automatically lets the response back out, no outbound rule needed. A NACL doesn't remember anything; it evaluates inbound and outbound independently every time. So if I only write the inbound allow rule on a NACL and forget the matching outbound rule for the ephemeral port range, the request gets in but the response never gets out, and from the client's perspective it just hangs. NACLs are also numbered and evaluated in order with first-match-wins, which is another way they behave completely differently from SGs' order-independent allow-only rules.
questions.example:
Security Group: one inbound rule for TCP 443 — stateful, response automatically allowed back out, no outbound rule needed.
Network ACL: inbound rule for TCP 443, PLUS a separate outbound rule allowing TCP 1024-65535 (ephemeral ports) — stateless, both directions need their own rule.
commonMistakes: Assuming a NACL behaves statefully the same way a Security Group does
Forgetting the ephemeral port range entirely when writing NACL rules
Not knowing NACL rules are numbered and evaluated in order, first match wins
Confusing a Security Group's instance-level scope with a NACL's subnet-level scope
keyPoints: Security Groups are stateful, instance-level, allow-only
Network ACLs are stateless, subnet-level, numbered allow/deny with first match winning
Stateless rules require an explicit outbound rule for the ephemeral port range
Most real designs use both layers together, not one instead of the other

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains stateful vs. stateless behavior
Correctly explains the ephemeral port rule requirement
Correctly distinguishes Security Group and NACL scope

lessonLink.label: Review: Security Groups vs. Network ACLs

questions.title: Encryption at rest vs. encryption in transit
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between encryption at rest and encryption in transit, and why does a cloud environment need both rather than just one or the other?
questions.modelAnswer: Encryption at rest protects data while it's stored — on a disk, in a database, in object storage, in a backup — so that someone who somehow gets access to the raw storage medium or a stolen backup can't read the actual data without the encryption key. Encryption in transit (TLS) protects data while it's moving across a network, so someone intercepting the traffic between a client and a server can't read or tamper with it in flight. These protect against two completely different attack points: data encrypted at rest but sent in plaintext over the network is still exposed to eavesdropping, and data protected only in transit but stored unencrypted is still exposed if the storage or a backup is compromised. A key management service like Azure Key Vault or AWS KMS manages the keys behind at-rest encryption; TLS certificates handle the in-transit side.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as two different moments in a piece of data's life. At rest is about the data sitting still — on a disk, in a database file, in a backup — and encryption there protects against someone getting physical or logical access to that storage. In transit is about the data moving — a request going from a browser to a server — and TLS protects against someone intercepting that network traffic. I always point out that having one without the other leaves a real gap: encrypting a database at rest doesn't help at all if the application still sends that data over plain HTTP, and encrypting the network connection doesn't help if the database itself is sitting unencrypted and the storage gets compromised separately.
questions.example: A database storing customer records: encryption at rest (via a platform-managed or customer-managed key in Key Vault/KMS) protects the stored data files; TLS on the application's connection to that database protects the data as it's queried and returned over the network. Both layers are needed, since each protects against a different point of compromise.
commonMistakes: Assuming TLS alone covers 'encryption' for an entire system
Assuming all cloud storage is automatically encrypted without understanding what's platform-managed by default
Not distinguishing which specific threat each protects against
Confusing a key management service itself with the encryption it enables
keyPoints: Encryption at rest protects stored data from compromised storage or backups
Encryption in transit (TLS) protects moving data from network interception
Each protects against a different attack point — both are needed
Key Vault/KMS manage the keys behind at-rest encryption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines both encryption at rest and in transit
Explains why both are needed as separate protections
Mentions the role of a key management service

questions.title: What idempotent means for an automation script
questions.prompt: What does it mean for an infrastructure automation script to be idempotent, and why does this matter more in a CI/CD pipeline than it does when you're just running a script once by hand?
questions.modelAnswer: A script is idempotent if running it once, or running it five times in a row, leaves the infrastructure in exactly the same end state either way — it doesn't create duplicate resources and doesn't error out because something it's trying to create already exists. This matters far more in a pipeline than for a manual one-off run because pipelines retry failed steps and get rerun routinely, automatically, and without a human checking the current state first — a deployment pipeline retrying after an unrelated step failed, for instance, might re-run a provisioning script that already succeeded the first time. The standard fix is the check-then-act pattern: verify whether a resource already exists before deciding whether to create it, so reruns are always safe regardless of how often they happen.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat idempotency as mandatory for anything that's going to run in a pipeline, specifically because pipelines retry constantly and nobody is watching to confirm state first the way they might for a manual run. If a script blindly calls something like New-AzResourceGroup every time, it works the first time and then throws an error on any retry, because the resource already exists. The fix I always reach for is check-then-act: call something like Get-AzResourceGroup with -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue first, and only create the resource if that check comes back empty. That one pattern turns 'did this already run?' into a question that genuinely doesn't matter anymore.
commonMistakes: Thinking idempotent means a script should only ever be run once
Not recognizing pipelines retry and rerun far more often than manual execution
Assuming a try/catch that swallows the error is the same as actually checking for existence first
Forgetting the check-then-act pattern applies to every kind of resource, not just the one example seen in training
keyPoints: Idempotent = same end state whether run once or many times
Check-then-act is the standard idempotent pattern
Pipelines retry and rerun automatically and routinely
A non-idempotent script fails or duplicates resources on rerun

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a correct definition of idempotent
Explains the pipeline-specific risk clearly
Describes the check-then-act pattern

lessonLink.label: Review: Idempotency

questions.title: RTO vs. RPO
questions.prompt: What do RTO and RPO each actually measure, and why is it wrong to say a nightly backup job 'satisfies' a 1-hour RPO just because the backups have never failed?
questions.modelAnswer: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) measures how long a system can be down before that downtime becomes genuinely unacceptable to the business — it's a question about tolerable outage length. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) measures how much data loss, in time, is acceptable if you have to restore from a backup — a question about tolerable data loss. A nightly-only backup schedule can never satisfy a 1-hour RPO, no matter how reliably it runs, because the worst-case data loss with a daily job is a full day, not an hour — RPO is about the maximum possible gap between successful backups, not whether any individual backup succeeds. The fix is to configure backups to run at least as often as the RPO requires, before ever configuring a backup policy, not after picking a schedule that happens to be convenient.
questions.professionalAnswer: I keep these as two separate questions in my head: how long can we be down (RTO), and how much data can we afford to lose (RPO). A team that says 'we do nightly backups, so our RPO is fine' has the logic backwards — reliability and frequency aren't the same thing. Even a nightly job that has never once failed still has a worst-case data-loss window of almost 24 hours, because the gap between backups is what defines the RPO, not the backup's success rate. If the business actually needs a 1-hour RPO, the schedule has to run at least every hour, full stop — there's no version of 'reliable but infrequent' that gets you there. I also always remind people RTO has to include the time it takes to even notice the outage and start the restore, not just the restore itself.
questions.example: Business says: "We can lose at most 1 hour of order data." -> RPO = 1 hour -> backups must run at least every 60 minutes; a nightly-only schedule does NOT meet this, regardless of reliability.
commonMistakes: Treating RTO and RPO as one combined 'how bad can it get' number
Thinking a highly reliable backup job automatically satisfies any RPO
Picking a convenient backup schedule first, then calling it the RPO after the fact
Forgetting RTO includes the time to detect and begin responding to an outage, not just the restore itself
keyPoints: RTO = how long a system can tolerate being down
RPO = how much data loss is tolerable, measured in time since the last good backup
RPO requires backup frequency at least as often as the RPO window
RTO and RPO should be set before configuring any backup policy, not derived from a convenient schedule

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines RTO and RPO
Correctly explains why a nightly backup fails a 1-hour RPO
Notes RTO includes detection/response time, not just restore time

lessonLink.label: Review: RTO and RPO

questions.title: Object, block, and file storage
questions.prompt: What are the three main categories of cloud storage, and what specific need does each one solve that the other two genuinely can't?
questions.modelAnswer: Object storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage) stores whole objects in a flat, API-driven structure with no real folder hierarchy — great for unstructured data like backups, logs, and static assets, but it can't be mounted like a drive. Block storage (AWS EBS, Azure Managed Disks) presents raw, fixed-size blocks that attach to one VM like a physical hard drive, offering low latency for a database's data files or an OS boot volume, but it's normally attached to exactly one VM at a time. File storage (AWS EFS, Azure Files) is a real hierarchical filesystem accessed over a network protocol like NFS or SMB, and its defining feature is that multiple VMs can mount the same share simultaneously — the one need neither object nor block storage solves.
questions.professionalAnswer: I pick between these based on access pattern, not raw speed. If I need to store something read and written by one application via an API — backups, logs, static files — that's object storage, and S3 or Blob Storage is effectively infinitely scalable for it. If I need a fast disk attached to one specific VM — a database's data files, an OS boot volume — that's block storage, EBS or Managed Disks, but I'm careful that it's normally a single-VM attachment, not something I can hand to three servers at once. If several app servers behind a load balancer all need to read and write the same shared files at the same time, neither of the other two works — that's exactly the case file storage like EFS or Azure Files exists to solve.
questions.example:
Backups/logs/static files -> object storage (S3, Blob Storage).
OS boot volume or database files for one VM -> block storage (EBS, Managed Disks).
Shared uploads directory mounted by three web servers at once -> file storage (EFS, Azure Files).
commonMistakes: Trying to mount object storage like a drive
Using block storage expecting multiple VMs to share it by default
Forgetting file storage's simultaneous multi-mount capability is its entire reason to exist
Assuming one storage type is simply 'the best' regardless of the actual access pattern needed
keyPoints: Object storage = flat, API-accessed, built for unstructured data (S3, Blob Storage)
Block storage = raw disk attached to one VM (EBS, Managed Disks)
File storage = shared hierarchical filesystem multiple VMs mount at once (EFS, Azure Files)
The deciding factor is access pattern, not just performance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines all three storage types
Correctly identifies the distinguishing use case for each
Gives accurate real-world product examples

questions.title: Calculating usable hosts in a subnet
questions.prompt: You're given the subnet 10.0.5.0/28. Walk through how many host bits it has, how many total addresses that gives you, how many of those are actually usable by devices, and what the first and last usable host addresses are.
questions.modelAnswer: A /28 leaves 32 - 28 = 4 host bits, giving 2^4 = 16 total addresses. Subtracting the 2 reserved addresses — the network address and the broadcast address — leaves 14 usable host addresses. The network address is 10.0.5.0 (reserved, identifies the subnet), so the first usable host is 10.0.5.1, and the broadcast address is the very last address in the range, 10.0.5.15, making the last usable host 10.0.5.14.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always start with the host-bit math: 32 total bits minus the prefix length gives the host bits, so a /28 has 4. Two to the power of that is 16 total addresses in the subnet. Every subnet reserves its first address as the network address and its last as the broadcast address, so I subtract 2 from the total to get usable hosts — 14 here. From there the first usable host is just the network address plus one (10.0.5.1), and the last usable host is the broadcast address minus one (10.0.5.14), with 10.0.5.15 itself reserved for broadcast.
questions.example:
32 - 28 = 4 host bits
2^4 = 16 total addresses
16 - 2 (network + broadcast) = 14 usable hosts
Network address: 10.0.5.0 (reserved)
First usable host: 10.0.5.1
Last usable host: 10.0.5.14
Broadcast address: 10.0.5.15 (reserved)
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract the 2 reserved addresses from the total
Miscalculating host bits (32 minus the prefix length)
Assuming the broadcast address is the second-to-last address instead of the actual last one
Applying /24 assumptions to a subnet with a different prefix length
keyPoints: Host bits = 32 minus the prefix length
Total addresses = 2 raised to the host-bit count
Usable hosts = total addresses minus 2 (network + broadcast)
First usable host = network address + 1; last usable host = broadcast address - 1

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct host-bit and total-address math
Correct usable-host count
Correct first and last usable host addresses

questions.title: Fixing a Linux permissions problem
questions.prompt: A deployment script `deploy.sh` currently shows `rw-r--r--` when you run `ls -l`. The owner needs to be able to execute it; the group and everyone else should keep their current read-only access. What single `chmod` command, in octal, fixes this, and what will the resulting permission string look like?
questions.code:
$ ls -l deploy.sh
-rw-r--r--  1 jsmith developers  812 Oct 28 09:00 deploy.sh
questions.modelAnswer: rw-r--r-- breaks into owner=rw- (4+2=6), group=r-- (4), other=r-- (4), which is octal 644. The owner needs execute added on top of their existing read/write, making their triplet rwx (4+2+1=7), while group and other stay unchanged at r-- (4) each. That gives octal 744, applied with `chmod 744 deploy.sh`, and the resulting permission string is `rwxr--r--`.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd work it out digit by digit rather than guessing. The current string rw-r--r-- is 644 in octal — owner 6 (rw-), group 4 (r--), other 4 (r--). The only change needed is adding execute to the owner's triplet, and execute is worth 1, so 6 becomes 7 (rwx). Group and other don't change at all, so the command is `chmod 744 deploy.sh`, and I'd always follow it with `ls -l` to confirm the result actually reads `rwxr--r--` before trusting it.
questions.example:
$ chmod 744 deploy.sh
$ ls -l deploy.sh
-rwxr--r--  1 jsmith developers  812 Oct 28 09:00 deploy.sh
commonMistakes: Using `chmod +x` without considering it may also affect group or other depending on context, instead of the precise octal value needed
Miscalculating the octal value for one or more of the triplets
Forgetting to verify the result with `ls -l` after changing permissions
Confusing `chmod` (permissions) with `chown` (ownership) when only permissions need to change
keyPoints: rwx maps to octal values 4 (read), 2 (write), 1 (execute), summed per triplet
The three octal digits map directly to owner, group, and other
chmod 744 = owner rwx, group r--, other r--
Always verify the change with ls -l afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct octal calculation
Correct resulting permission string
Correct chmod command syntax

questions.title: Giving an EC2 instance S3 access without any access keys
questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, how you'd give an EC2 instance read access to one specific S3 bucket without ever generating or storing an access key anywhere, from creating the IAM role through confirming the application can actually read the bucket.
questions.modelAnswer: First, create an IAM policy that grants s3:GetObject (and s3:ListBucket if the app needs to enumerate objects) scoped specifically to that one bucket's ARN, not every bucket in the account. Next, create an IAM role whose trust policy allows the EC2 service to assume it, and attach the policy to that role. Then attach the role to the EC2 instance as an instance profile, either at launch or afterward. The application running on the instance uses the default credential provider chain — which automatically picks up the role's temporary credentials through the instance metadata service — so no access key ever needs to be generated or placed in code. Finally, confirm it works by running an S3 call from the instance (like `aws s3 ls s3://bucket-name`) with no local credentials configured at all, and verifying it succeeds.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it in the order it actually gets built. Policy first: scope it to exactly the one bucket's ARN and only the actions actually needed, not a blanket S3 policy. Role next: the trust policy has to explicitly allow the EC2 service to assume it, or EC2 simply can't use it. Then I attach that role to the instance as an instance profile — easy to forget this step even after the role exists, since creating the role alone doesn't attach it to anything. On the instance itself, I don't configure any credentials at all; the SDK or CLI picks up the role's temporary credentials automatically through the instance metadata service. The real confirmation is running a real S3 call from the instance and seeing it succeed with zero credentials configured locally — that's the proof there's no static key sitting anywhere.
questions.example:
1. IAM policy: {"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:ListBucket"],"Resource":["arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket","arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"]}
2. IAM role with trust policy allowing ec2.amazonaws.com to assume it, policy attached.
3. Attach the role to the EC2 instance as an instance profile.
4. From the instance: aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket -- succeeds with no local credentials configured.
commonMistakes: Generating an access key 'just in case' and embedding it anyway, defeating the whole point
Forgetting the trust policy, without which EC2 simply can't assume the role
Scoping the policy to every bucket in the account instead of the one specific bucket's ARN
Creating the role but forgetting to actually attach it to the instance as an instance profile
keyPoints: The policy grants only the specific actions needed, scoped to the one bucket's ARN
The trust policy defines who or what can assume the role — here, the EC2 service
The role is attached to the instance via an instance profile
The application uses the default credential chain automatically, with no static keys anywhere

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct end-to-end sequence of steps
Correctly scoped, least-privilege policy
Clearly explains why no static keys are ever needed

questions.title: Writing an Azure NSG rule for HTTPS
questions.prompt: Using the Azure CLI, write the command to add an inbound NSG rule named `Allow-HTTPS` to an NSG called `web-nsg` in resource group `rg-web`, allowing TCP port 443 from any source, with priority 100.
questions.code: # Resource group rg-web and NSG web-nsg already exist, with no custom rules yet.
questions.modelAnswer: `az network nsg rule create` needs the NSG name, resource group, rule name, priority, direction, access decision, protocol, destination port range, and source. Priority 100 means this rule is evaluated early (lower numbers are evaluated first), direction is Inbound, access is Allow, protocol is Tcp, the destination port range is 443, and the source is set to allow any address.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the full command naming every required parameter explicitly rather than relying on defaults, since NSG rule defaults have changed across CLI versions and I don't want to guess. Priority 100 puts it near the front of the evaluation order, which matters because NSGs evaluate rules in ascending priority order and stop at the first match. Allowing from '*' is a deliberate choice here because the prompt asked for 'any source' — in a real environment I'd push back and ask whether that's genuinely intended, since an open-to-the-internet rule is worth a second look even when it's just for HTTPS.
questions.example:
az network nsg rule create \
  --nsg-name web-nsg \
  --resource-group rg-web \
  --name Allow-HTTPS \
  --priority 100 \
  --direction Inbound \
  --access Allow \
  --protocol Tcp \
  --destination-port-ranges 443 \
  --source-address-prefixes '*'
commonMistakes: Omitting --direction Inbound and assuming a default that may not match intent
Choosing a priority number that collides with an existing rule
Opening the rule to '*' without stopping to consider whether that's actually the intended design
Forgetting NSG rules are evaluated in ascending priority order, lowest number first
keyPoints: az network nsg rule create requires nsg-name, resource-group, name, priority, direction, access, protocol, port, and source
Lower priority numbers are evaluated first
Source '*' means from anywhere — a deliberate design choice, not a default to accept blindly
Confirm the result with az network nsg rule list after creating it

Correct priority, direction, and access values
Notes the security implication of an open-to-anywhere source

questions.title: Writing an idempotent resource-group creation check
questions.prompt: This PowerShell line creates an Azure resource group but fails with an error the second time it's run: `New-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-prod" -Location "eastus"`. Rewrite it so the script is safe to run any number of times.
questions.code:
# NOT idempotent -- fails on the second run
New-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-prod" -Location "eastus"
questions.modelAnswer: Wrap the creation in a check that looks for the resource group first, using `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` so the check itself doesn't throw an error when the resource group doesn't exist yet, and only call `New-AzResourceGroup` inside the branch where that check comes back empty.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd apply the standard check-then-act pattern here: call `Get-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-prod" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` first, which quietly returns nothing instead of throwing an error if the resource group isn't there yet. Then I only call `New-AzResourceGroup` inside an `if (-not (...))` block guarding that check. The result is a script that creates the resource group on the first run and does nothing — no error, no duplicate — on every run after that, which is exactly what makes it safe to leave in a pipeline that might retry it.
commonMistakes: Calling New-AzResourceGroup unconditionally with no existence check at all
Omitting -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue, causing the check itself to throw when the resource group doesn't exist
Wrapping the original call in a try/catch that swallows the error instead of checking first
Not recognizing this exact pattern needs to be applied to every other 'create' call in a larger script, not just this one
keyPoints: The check-then-act pattern is the standard idempotent fix
-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue lets the existence check fail quietly instead of throwing
Only call the create cmdlet inside the branch where the check found nothing
This exact pattern generalizes to any resource type, not just resource groups

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct check-then-act logic
Correct PowerShell syntax
Explains why this makes the script idempotent

questions.title: Tagging a resource group and knowing what policy adds
questions.prompt: Using Azure CLI, apply the tags `Environment=Production` and `CostCenter=1000` to an existing resource group called `rg-prod-eastus-web01`. Then, in one or two sentences, explain the difference between what that tag does and what an Azure Policy assignment requiring that tag would do.
questions.code: # rg-prod-eastus-web01 already exists with no tags set.
questions.modelAnswer: `az group update` with `--set tags` applies the two tags to the existing resource group. Tags are pure metadata — they don't enforce anything by themselves, they just power filtering and cost reporting. An Azure Policy assignment requiring that tag would actively enforce it: a deployment missing the required tag would be blocked (a Deny effect) at the ARM layer before the resource is even created, rather than just being flagged after the fact in a report.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the tagging itself, I'd use `az group update --name rg-prod-eastus-web01 --set tags.Environment=Production tags.CostCenter=1000` since the resource group already exists — the `--tags` flag on `az group create` only applies at creation time. On the conceptual question, I always draw a hard line between the two: a tag is metadata that does nothing unless something else reads it, like Cost Management grouping spend by CostCenter. A policy is enforcement — assign a built-in policy requiring the CostCenter tag, and any deployment missing it gets blocked outright, failing before the resource is ever created, not caught later in a compliance report.
questions.example: az group update --name rg-prod-eastus-web01 --set tags.Environment=Production tags.CostCenter=1000
commonMistakes: Confusing tags (pure metadata) with policy (active enforcement)
Using az group create's --tags syntax against an already-existing resource group
Assuming tags alone prevent a non-compliant deployment from succeeding
Not naming a concrete policy effect (Deny, Audit) when explaining what enforcement actually looks like

Azure Policy actively enforces rules, with effects like Deny, Audit, Append, or DeployIfNotExists
Tags power cost reporting and resource filtering
Policy can block a deployment entirely before the resource is created

questions.title: Uploading an S3 object to the right storage class
questions.prompt: Using the AWS CLI, write the command to upload a local file `2025-archive.tar.gz` to the bucket `ltv-academy-media-backups` under the key `archive/2025-archive.tar.gz`, using the cheapest storage class appropriate for data you're very unlikely to ever need in a hurry. Then explain the cost/retrieval tradeoff behind that choice.
questions.modelAnswer: `aws s3 cp ./2025-archive.tar.gz s3://ltv-academy-media-backups/archive/2025-archive.tar.gz --storage-class GLACIER` uploads it directly to Glacier. The tradeoff: S3 Glacier is by far the cheapest storage class, but retrieval takes anywhere from minutes to hours depending on the retrieval tier chosen, which is acceptable for data you're genuinely unlikely to need in a hurry but would be the wrong choice for anything that might need to come back quickly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run the upload with `--storage-class GLACIER` directly, since 'unlikely to ever need in a hurry' is exactly the description Glacier is built for — it trades retrieval speed for the lowest possible storage cost. I'd distinguish this from S3 Standard-IA, which still gives millisecond retrieval but charges a per-GB retrieval fee and costs more to store than Glacier — the right pick for data you need fast *if* someone asks for it, but rarely do. Glacier is the right pick here specifically because the scenario describes data that's unlikely to be retrieved in a hurry at all, not just infrequently.
questions.example:
aws s3 cp ./2025-archive.tar.gz \
  s3://ltv-academy-media-backups/archive/2025-archive.tar.gz \
  --storage-class GLACIER
commonMistakes: Choosing Standard-IA when the scenario specifically calls for Glacier's deeper cost/speed tradeoff
Forgetting the --storage-class flag defaults to S3 Standard if omitted
Not mentioning that retrieval fees apply even to data that's rarely read
Assuming the 'key' requires a real folder to exist first, rather than just being a string
keyPoints: aws s3 cp --storage-class GLACIER for rarely-needed archive data
S3 Standard-IA is the middle tier: cheaper storage, still millisecond access, per-GB retrieval fee
Glacier trades retrieval speed for the lowest possible storage cost
An object's key is just a string; S3's namespace underneath is flat

Correctly distinguishes Glacier from Standard-IA

questions.title: Reordering a Dockerfile for faster rebuilds
questions.prompt: This Dockerfile rebuilds `npm ci` from scratch on every single code change, even when `package.json` hasn't changed. Rewrite it so the dependency-install layer stays cached across source-only changes.
questions.code:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
questions.modelAnswer: Copy only the dependency manifest files first, run `npm ci` against just those, and only then copy the rest of the source code. Because Docker caches each instruction's layer and reuses it as long as its inputs are unchanged, this means `npm ci` only reruns when `package.json` or `package-lock.json` actually change — editing `server.js` now only invalidates the final `COPY . .` layer, leaving the slower dependency-install layer cached.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fix is pure instruction reordering: copy `package.json` and `package-lock.json` by themselves first, run `npm ci` right after, and only then copy the rest of the application source. Docker's layer cache works by diffing each instruction's inputs against the last build — as long as those two manifest files haven't changed, the `npm ci` layer stays cached no matter how much `server.js` has changed, because that `COPY . .` line comes after it now, not before.
questions.example:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
commonMistakes: Copying the entire source directory before installing dependencies
Forgetting to also copy package-lock.json alongside package.json
Not understanding that once one layer's cache misses, every layer after it rebuilds too
Assuming a later cleanup step can shrink bytes that were already committed in an earlier layer
keyPoints: Docker reuses a cached layer only while its instruction and inputs are unchanged
Once one layer's cache misses, every layer built on top of it reruns too
Copy dependency manifests and install dependencies before copying the rest of the source
This same pattern applies to pip, go mod, and any other ecosystem's dependency step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reorders the COPY/RUN instructions
Explains why this preserves the dependency-install layer's cache
Copies both manifest files needed before running npm ci

questions.title: Checking a DNS record with dig
questions.prompt: You need to confirm what IP address `www.example.com` currently resolves to, and how much longer that answer will stay cached before a resolver has to re-check it. What command would you run, and how do you read the two relevant pieces of its output?
questions.code: # Need to confirm the current A record and remaining TTL for www.example.com
questions.modelAnswer: Run `dig www.example.com` and read the ANSWER SECTION: the record's type (A), its IP address, and the number immediately before the record type, which is the remaining TTL in seconds — proof the answer came from cache and hasn't fully expired yet. `dig www.example.com +short` strips everything down to just the IP address, which is handy for scripts but hides the TTL.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run `dig www.example.com` because it shows the mechanics in one shot. In the ANSWER SECTION, the line reads something like `www.example.com. 299 IN A 93.184.216.34` — the `299` is the remaining TTL in seconds, counting down from whatever value the record was published with, and `93.184.216.34` is the actual IP it currently resolves to. If I just need the address for a script, `dig www.example.com +short` gives me that alone, but I'd use the full output here specifically because the TTL is part of what's being asked.
questions.example:
;; ANSWER SECTION:
www.example.com.    299    IN    A    93.184.216.34
-- IP address: 93.184.216.34
-- Remaining TTL: 299 seconds
commonMistakes: Using nslookup and misreading 'non-authoritative answer' as an error instead of a sign the answer came from cache
Treating the TTL number as a fixed constant instead of a countdown remaining from the last publish
Using dig +short when the TTL is actually part of what's needed
Forgetting a CNAME chain has to be followed to its final A record before there's a usable IP
keyPoints: dig <name> shows the ANSWER SECTION with record type and IP
The number before the record type is the remaining TTL in seconds
nslookup's 'non-authoritative answer' means the result came from a resolver's cache
dig +short strips the output down to just the address, dropping TTL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct command
Correctly reads the IP address from the output
Correctly reads and explains the TTL field

questions.title: SSH hangs after an office move
questions.prompt: A Linux VM in Azure was reachable last week. Today, SSH just hangs with no response at all — no 'connection refused,' no error. The VM shows as running in the portal. What's your diagnostic order, and what's the most likely root cause given that it 'used to work, now it just silently hangs'?
questions.modelAnswer: Start broad and narrow down: first confirm the VM is actually running, which rules out a boot failure. Next, check the NSG rules on the subnet or NIC, specifically the source address range on the allow-SSH rule — a silent hang with no error at all is the classic signature of an NSG quietly dropping the traffic rather than an OS-level problem, which would usually produce some kind of response or error. Check the route table next to rule out a routing change. Only after those cloud-layer checks come back clean would I move to the OS layer (systemctl status sshd, /var/log/auth.log). Given 'it used to work, now it silently hangs,' the most likely cause is a stale NSG rule whose allowed source IP range no longer matches the client's current public IP — for example after an office move changed the outbound IP the SSH traffic is actually coming from.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd work broad to narrow rather than guessing at the OS first. VM running? Yes, so it's not a boot problem. Next I go straight to the NSG, because a silent hang with zero response is almost always a network-layer block, not an application error — if sshd itself had rejected the connection, I'd expect some kind of response, not dead silence. I'd specifically check whether the allowed source IP range on the SSH rule still matches where the traffic is actually coming from, since 'worked last week, doesn't now' with no config change on the VM side points straight at something changing on the network side instead — an office's outbound IP changing is the textbook version of this. I'd only drop into the OS and check auth.log last, and if I did, an empty log with zero attempts logged would confirm the traffic never even arrived.
questions.example: Office IP changed from 203.0.113.0/24 to 198.51.100.0/24. The Allow-SSH NSG rule still only permits 203.0.113.0/24, so the new office's traffic never matches the rule and gets silently dropped -- no error, just a hang.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight into OS-level troubleshooting (sshd config, auth.log) before checking the network layer
Assuming a 'running' VM status rules out a silent network-level block
Not recognizing a silent hang (vs. an explicit refusal) as a strong network-layer signal
Forgetting that an empty auth.log (zero attempts at all) proves traffic never arrived, which is different from failed attempts proving it arrived but authentication failed
keyPoints: Diagnose broad to narrow: VM state, then network/NSG, then OS/service
A silent hang with no response usually means traffic never reached the VM at all
NSG rules go stale when a client's actual source IP changes
An empty auth.log (no attempts logged) confirms the traffic never arrived

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct diagnostic order, broad to narrow
Correctly identifies a stale NSG rule as the most likely root cause
Explains the empty auth.log evidence correctly

questions.title: An unexplained Azure cost spike
questions.prompt: Finance flags that this month's Azure bill is three times normal, with no known new project launched. What's your systematic approach to finding the cause, and what are two or three of the most common real-world causes of a surprise cost spike like this?
questions.modelAnswer: Start in Cost Management's Cost Analysis view, broken down by resource group or by tag like Environment or CostCenter, to find which specific area of spend actually grew. Cross-reference that with the Activity Log to see what resources were created or resized recently, since the spike has to trace back to some actual change. Common real-world causes: a forgotten test or sandbox VM (or scale set) left running past when it should have been torn down, an autoscale rule that scaled up under load and never scaled back down, or an oversized VM SKU chosen without right-sizing. If no budget or cost alert existed before this, that's also worth flagging as the preventive gap that let the spike go unnoticed for a full month.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go straight to Cost Analysis and break the bill down by tag or resource group first, since 'the whole bill tripled' is too broad to act on — I need to know which specific thing grew. Once I've localized it, I'd check the Activity Log around that resource group for anything created or resized recently, because a 3x spike doesn't happen without some actual change somewhere. In my experience the usual suspects are a test VM or scale set someone forgot to tear down, an autoscale rule that scaled up during a traffic spike and was never configured to scale back down, or a VM SKU that was oversized from the start and nobody right-sized it. I'd also flag that if there was no budget or cost alert set up beforehand, that's the real gap — it's why nobody caught this until the invoice arrived instead of a week into it.
questions.example: Cost Analysis grouped by resource group shows rg-sandbox-test accounts for 60% of this month's spend, despite no production workload running there. Activity Log confirms a scale set was created there three weeks ago for a test and never deleted.
commonMistakes: Assuming the spike must be a billing error rather than investigating actual resource usage
Not using tags or resource groups to localize which area of spend actually grew
Skipping the Activity Log and missing what was actually deployed recently
Not setting up a budget alert afterward to catch a similar spike earlier next time
keyPoints: Use Cost Analysis grouped by tag or resource group to localize the spike
Cross-reference with the Activity Log for recent deployments or resizes
Common causes: forgotten test resources, runaway autoscale, oversized SKUs
Set up a budget and cost alert afterward to catch it earlier next time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a systematic investigation approach
Names plausible, realistic causes
Mentions a preventive step (budget/alert) for next time

questions.title: An EC2 instance that's suddenly unreachable
questions.prompt: An EC2 instance that was working fine yesterday is now unreachable over SSH, and the team insists 'nothing changed.' Walk through how you'd narrow this down to the actual cause.
questions.modelAnswer: First check the instance's status checks in the console to rule out a host-level failure. Next verify the security group's inbound rule for port 22 and its source CIDR are still correct. Then check the subnet's route table to confirm a route to the internet gateway still exists, since someone might have modified it thinking it was unrelated. A detail that's easy to miss: if the instance was stopped and started (rather than just rebooted) without an Elastic IP attached, it gets a brand-new public IP, which would make the old IP everyone's using unreachable even though nothing about the instance's configuration actually broke. Only after exhausting those checks would I move to OS-level troubleshooting via EC2 Instance Connect or the system log. 'Nothing changed' often really means 'nothing I'm aware of changed,' so checking CloudTrail for recent changes made by anyone is a reasonable early step too.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't take 'nothing changed' at face value — I check CloudTrail for what actually happened recently, because it usually means 'nothing *I* changed.' Beyond that, I'd check instance status checks first to rule out a host-level issue, then the security group's inbound rule and source CIDR, then the route table to confirm there's still a route out to the internet gateway. The gotcha I always check specifically: did this instance get stopped and started recently without an Elastic IP? Because that silently assigns a new public IP, and if everyone's still trying to connect to the old one, it'll look exactly like 'suddenly unreachable' even though the instance itself is perfectly healthy.
questions.example: The instance was stopped overnight for a patch and started again without an attached Elastic IP. Its public IP changed from 52.14.x.x to 54.91.x.x. The team is still trying the old IP, which now points at nothing.
commonMistakes: Taking 'nothing changed' at face value instead of checking CloudTrail for recent activity
Forgetting that stopping and starting an instance without an Elastic IP assigns it a new public IP
Jumping straight into OS-level troubleshooting before checking status checks, security groups, and routing
Not checking instance status checks first to rule out a host-level failure
keyPoints: Check instance status checks first to rule out a host-level issue
Verify the security group's inbound rule and source CIDR
Verify the route table still has a route to the internet gateway
Stopping and starting an instance without an Elastic IP changes its public IP
'Nothing changed' often means 'nothing I know of changed' — check CloudTrail

questions.title: Remediating a CSPM finding without breaking anything
questions.prompt: Your cloud security posture management tool flags a storage account as 'publicly accessible — high severity.' Before you just flip the setting to private, what should you check first, and why might blindly disabling public access actually break something?
questions.modelAnswer: Check first what, or who, is actually currently using that public access — reviewing access logs and asking the resource owner whether there's a legitimate reason, like static website hosting or a partner integration pulling files directly. A storage account can be publicly accessible by design, not just by accident, and blindly flipping it to private could take down a live website, break an integration, or fail a scheduled job that pulls public files — an outage that's arguably worse than the original finding. Once confirmed there's no legitimate need, the right fix is restricting access appropriately (private with SAS tokens, or a CDN/Private Endpoint if some form of public delivery is still genuinely required) and documenting the change.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is never the fix itself — it's finding out who or what actually depends on the current setting. I'd check access logs for recent activity and ask the resource owner directly whether public access was intentional, since a static website or a partner data feed can legitimately need it. If I flip it to private without checking, I could take down a live site or silently break an integration that's been quietly working for months, which turns a security finding into a real incident. Once I've confirmed there's no legitimate reason, I'd remediate properly — private access plus SAS tokens, or a CDN or Private Endpoint if some public delivery is still genuinely needed — and I'd always loop in the resource owner before making the change, not after.
questions.example: The storage account turns out to host static marketing assets served directly to a public website via its public endpoint. Disabling public access without checking would have broken that website immediately. The proper fix is routing that delivery through a CDN instead, then locking the storage account down.

Assuming every CSPM 'high severity' finding needs an identical, immediate fix regardless of context
Not communicating the change to the resource owner before applying it
Forgetting a legitimate static-website or CDN use case can look identical to an accidental misconfiguration

Distinguish legitimate public use (static site, CDN) from accidental exposure
Consider safer alternatives (Private Endpoint, CDN, SAS tokens) if public delivery is genuinely needed
Communicate with the resource owner before changing a live setting

questions.title: A provisioning script fails the second time it runs
questions.prompt: A PowerShell script that creates an Azure storage account worked the first time it ran in a pipeline. The pipeline then automatically retried it after an unrelated step failed, and now the entire run fails with 'storage account already exists.' What's actually wrong with the script, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The script isn't idempotent — it calls something like `New-AzStorageAccount` unconditionally, with no check for whether the storage account already exists. The fix is the same check-then-act pattern used for any resource: call `Get-AzStorageAccount -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` first, and only create the storage account inside the branch where that check comes back empty. This is exactly why pipelines specifically need idempotent scripts — automatic retries are routine, not a rare edge case, so any 'create' step without a check-first pattern will eventually hit this exact failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: This isn't a pipeline bug, it's a missing idempotency check in the script itself. The fix is the standard check-then-act pattern: `Get-AzStorageAccount -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` first, and only call the create cmdlet if that check comes back empty. I'd also treat this as a signal to audit the rest of the script — if this one 'create' call wasn't idempotent, there's a good chance other create steps in the same script have the identical gap, and they just haven't been hit by a retry yet.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a one-off fluke instead of a structural idempotency gap
Adding a try/catch that swallows the error instead of actually checking existence first
Not recognizing that pipeline retries happen automatically and routinely
Forgetting to audit the rest of the script for the same missing-check pattern

The fix is check-then-act: verify existence before creating
Pipelines retry automatically, so every provisioning step needs this pattern
Audit the rest of the script for the same gap elsewhere

questions.title: Applying the five-places framework to a new symptom
questions.prompt: A new VM was just deployed, and a teammate reports: 'the app on it can reach the database fine by IP address, but it can't resolve the database's hostname by name at all.' Which of the common deployment-failure categories does this fall into, and what would you check first?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a DNS resolution problem, not network/routing or security-group related — raw IP connectivity already working proves routing and security rules are fine. Check first whether a private DNS zone is configured for the environment and whether it's actually linked to the VNet the new VM lives in, since an unlinked zone is the most common reason a hostname that resolves fine elsewhere fails to resolve from a newly deployed resource. Since IP connectivity already works, there's no need to re-check NSGs or route tables — that's already proven fine.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd rule things out by what's already working: IP connectivity succeeding tells me routing and security groups are fine, which immediately narrows this to the DNS category rather than network or permissions. My first check is whether the environment's private DNS zone is actually linked to the VNet this new VM was deployed into — that's the single most common reason a hostname resolves everywhere except a newly created resource. I wouldn't waste time re-checking NSGs or route tables here; the symptom itself already proved those layers are working.
questions.example: The private DNS zone 'internal.ltv.local' is linked to vnet-app-prod but the new VM was deployed into vnet-app-dr, which was never linked to that zone. The hostname resolves fine from any VM in vnet-app-prod but fails from the new one.
commonMistakes: Re-checking NSGs or routing even though working IP connectivity already proves those layers are fine
Not considering an unlinked private DNS zone as the likely gap
Assuming the problem must be IAM/RBAC when the symptom clearly isn't an access-denied error
Jumping to OS-level DNS config before checking the cloud-side private DNS zone link
keyPoints: The five common deployment-failure categories: network/routing, security rules, DNS, IAM/RBAC, quota/limits
Working IP connectivity already rules out the network and security-group categories
This specific symptom points at DNS, most likely an unlinked private DNS zone
Triage using what's already proven to work before touching anything

Correctly reasons why network/security are already ruled out
Proposes the specific private DNS zone link check

questions.title: Why a DNS change doesn't show up everywhere at once
questions.prompt: You updated a domain's A record to point at a new IP two hours ago, and the change is definitely live on the authoritative server. A user on the other side of the country still reaches the old server. What's actually going on, and what should have been done before making the change?
questions.modelAnswer: That user's resolver is still serving a cached answer from before the change, and it stays valid until the cached record's TTL expires — if the old record was published with a high TTL (say, 86400 seconds), resolvers around the world can keep answering with the old IP for up to a full day after the authoritative record actually changed. The fix for next time is lowering the TTL well in advance of the planned cutover — days, not hours — so cached copies everywhere expire quickly once the real change happens.
questions.professionalAnswer: This isn't a mysterious 'propagation delay' — it's just caching doing exactly what it's supposed to do. That user's resolver cached the old answer and won't ask again until its TTL runs out, regardless of how quickly the authoritative server itself updated. If the old record had a 24-hour TTL, some resolvers can legitimately keep serving the old IP for nearly a full day. The move I'd make before any planned cutover is lowering the TTL days in advance, so by the time the actual change happens, cached copies everywhere are already set to expire quickly instead of lingering for a day.
questions.example: Old record: 300-second TTL lowered to 60 seconds three days before the cutover. On cutover day, cached copies everywhere expire within about a minute instead of lingering for hours.
commonMistakes: Assuming updating the authoritative server means everyone sees the change immediately
Not checking what TTL the old record was published with before planning the cutover
Lowering the TTL at the same time as the change instead of well in advance
Treating this as an unexplained 'propagation delay' rather than predictable caching behavior
keyPoints: DNS changes propagate only as fast as the old record's TTL allows caches to expire
Resolvers worldwide may still be serving the old cached answer for up to the old TTL
Lower the TTL days before a planned cutover, not at the time of the change
This is predictable caching behavior, not an unexplained mystery

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains TTL caching as the cause
Correctly explains why lowering the TTL in advance helps
Rejects the 'propagation just takes time' myth with a concrete mechanism

questions.title: A Docker image isn't picking up code changes
questions.prompt: A teammate edits `server.js`, rebuilds the Docker image, and runs the container — but it still behaves like the old code. `docker build` reports no errors and finishes quickly. What's the most likely explanation, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: A genuinely changed file should normally bust its COPY layer's cache on its own, so the most likely explanation isn't a stuck cache — it's that the running container isn't actually using the image that was just built. Either an old container from before is still running (never stopped and restarted), or the running `docker run` is referencing a stale tag that wasn't updated by the rebuild. Confirm by checking `docker images` for the build's timestamp to verify a fresh image was actually produced, and by running `docker inspect` on the currently running container to see exactly which image ID it's actually using, comparing that against the freshly built image's ID.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct isn't to blame Docker's cache — a real content change to `server.js` should invalidate that COPY layer automatically. I'd check whether the container that's actually running was ever stopped and restarted from the new image, since it's really common to rebuild an image and forget the old container is still happily running from before. I'd confirm by running `docker inspect` on the live container and comparing its image ID against the one `docker images` shows as the most recently built — if those don't match, that's the whole answer right there.
questions.example: docker images shows a fresh build from 2 minutes ago with image ID a1b2c3. docker inspect on the running container shows it's using image ID f9e8d7, built yesterday -- the container was never actually restarted from the new build.
commonMistakes: Assuming Docker's build cache is 'stuck' instead of checking whether the running container is actually using the new image
Not verifying which image ID the running container is actually using
Forgetting a genuinely changed file should normally invalidate its own COPY layer automatically
Not using docker images or docker inspect to verify what actually happened

The likelier cause is the running container isn't using the freshly built image at all
docker images shows build timestamps to confirm a fresh build happened
docker inspect on the running container reveals which image ID it's actually using

questions.title: A deployment fails with a policy error, not an access error
questions.prompt: An engineer tries to deploy a VM and gets an error referencing a policy, not an access-denied message. How is diagnosing this different from diagnosing an RBAC permission problem, and what's the first thing you'd check?
questions.modelAnswer: An RBAC failure means the caller lacks permission to perform the action at all — a true access-denied, 403-style response. A policy failure means the caller had permission to attempt the deployment, but the deployment's own properties violate an Azure Policy rule assigned at that scope (like a missing required tag or a disallowed VM SKU), and the policy engine blocked it at the ARM layer before the resource was ever created. The first thing to check is the actual error details — the specific policy and non-compliant property it names — rather than assuming it's a permission gap and trying to grant more roles, which wouldn't fix anything since permission was never the problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop myself from treating this like an RBAC issue, because the fix is completely different. RBAC failing means 'you can't do this at all.' Policy failing means 'you're allowed to try, but what you're trying to deploy breaks a rule' — a disallowed VM size, a missing tag, whatever that specific policy requires. I'd go straight to the error details or `az policy state list` to find exactly which policy fired and what property it's objecting to, since granting more roles would do absolutely nothing here — the caller already had permission the whole time.
questions.example: Error: "RequestDisallowedByPolicy ... policy definition 'Allowed virtual machine SKUs' ... Standard_D32s_v3 is not an allowed size." This is a policy block, not a permission problem -- the fix is choosing an allowed SKU, not granting a role.
commonMistakes: Treating a policy Deny the same as an RBAC permission gap and trying to grant more roles
Not checking the actual error details to identify the specific violated policy
Assuming every deployment failure is the same category of problem
Forgetting policy evaluates the resource's properties, not the caller's identity
keyPoints: RBAC failure = the caller lacks permission entirely
Policy failure = the caller has permission, but the resource's properties violate an assigned rule
Policy is enforced at the ARM layer, before the resource is ever created
Check the specific policy and non-compliant property in the error details first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes RBAC failures from policy failures
Correctly identifies the first diagnostic step
Explains policy's enforcement point at the ARM layer

questions.title: Diagnosing a permission gap after a deployment
questions.prompt: After a deployment, an application's managed identity can read from one storage account but not a newly added second one. The error message mentions 'authorization' rather than 'connection timed out' or 'not found.' What category of problem is this, and what's the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: This is an IAM/RBAC permission gap, confirmed by the error wording pointing at authorization rather than a network/DNS-style failure. The identity itself is fine — it already works against the first storage account — it's simply missing a role assignment on the new one, since role assignments are scoped per resource and don't carry over. The fix is assigning the managed identity the appropriate role (such as Storage Blob Data Reader) scoped to the new storage account, and verifying the fix with `az role assignment list` scoped to that resource before and after.
questions.professionalAnswer: The error wording is the clue I'd lean on immediately — 'authorization' points straight at IAM/RBAC, not network or DNS, which would read more like a timeout or a 'not found.' Since the identity already works fine against the first storage account, I know the identity itself isn't broken; it's just missing a role assignment scoped to the second one, because role assignments don't carry over between resources even for the same identity. The fix is adding the right role — something like Storage Blob Data Reader — scoped specifically to that new storage account, and I'd confirm it with `az role assignment list` both before making the change, to prove the gap, and after, to confirm it's fixed.
questions.example:
az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/rg-app/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/newstorageacct
-- confirms the managed identity has no role assignment on the new storage account, even though it has one on the original.
commonMistakes: Assuming the managed identity itself is broken rather than just missing a role assignment on the new resource
Troubleshooting network connectivity when the error text already points at authorization
Forgetting role assignments are scoped per resource, so access to one doesn't carry over to another
Not verifying the fix with az role assignment list before and after making the change
keyPoints: Error wording ('authorization' vs. 'timed out'/'not found') distinguishes IAM/RBAC issues from network or DNS issues
A role assignment is scoped — access to one resource doesn't carry over to another
The fix is adding the missing role assignment at the new resource's scope
Verify with az role assignment list both before and after the fix
